data.key_insight: Use two pointers moving at different speeds (one moving 1 step at a time, the other 2 steps). If there is a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually meet the slow pointer. If there is no cycle, the fast pointer will reach the end of the list.

steps.title: Initialize Pointers
steps.detail: Create two pointers, slow and fast, both initially pointing to the head of the linked list.

steps.title: Traverse the List
steps.detail: Iterate while the fast pointer and its next node are not null. Move the slow pointer by 1 step and the fast pointer by 2 steps.

steps.title: Check for Meeting Point
steps.detail: If at any point the slow pointer and fast pointer point to the same node, a cycle exists, so return true.

steps.title: Handle Termination
steps.detail: If the loop terminates because fast reaches the end (None), return false as there is no cycle.

data.pattern_summary: Store visited nodes in a collection as you traverse a data structure so you can check in constant time whether you have seen a node before.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Using a set to store references to visited nodes allows us to detect a loop efficiently.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: While a two-pointer approach works here for space optimization, the basic approach relies on tracking seen nodes.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: Dynamic programming is for problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, which does not apply to traversing a linked list.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices to find a global optimum, which is not relevant for cycle detection.

signals.phrase: Return true if there is a cycle in the linked list
signals.hint: Implies we need a way to detect if we revisit a node.

data.brute_force_idea: Traverse the linked list node by node, storing each visited node in a set. If we encounter a node that is already in the set, a cycle exists.
data.brute_force_why: We visit each node in the linked list at most once, performing constant time set lookups and insertions for each node.
data.bottleneck: The direct approach is already optimal in time complexity because every node in the cycle must be inspected at least once.
bottleneck_hints: Consider how many nodes you must inspect to be certain a cycle exists.
Can you traverse the list faster than visiting every node sequentially?
Since every node must be checked, O(n) time is the theoretical lower bound.

data.overview: Floyd's Cycle-Finding Algorithm uses two pointers moving at different speeds to detect cycles in a linked list. By having a slow pointer move 1 step and a fast pointer move 2 steps, they are guaranteed to meet if a cycle exists.
data.intuition: Imagine two runners on a circular track. The faster runner laps the slower runner eventually, whereas on a straight track the faster runner simply finishes first.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach uses extra memory in a hash set to keep track of every node visited, which bottlenecks space complexity. The optimized approach removes this storage requirement by using two pointers moving at different speeds. If a cycle exists, the faster pointer will eventually lap the slower pointer within the cycle.

derivation.note: The while loop runs proportional to the number of nodes until fast catches slow or hits the end.
Advances the slow pointer by one step per iteration.
Advances the fast pointer by two steps per iteration.
Compares pointer references on every iteration.

data.time_summary: Lines 3 and 4 run once for O(1) time. Lines 6 through 10 execute inside a loop that runs at most n times, scaling linearly with the input size. Thus, the total time complexity is O(n), confirmed by the measured steps scaling roughly linearly as n doubles.
data.space_summary: Only two pointer variables (slow and fast) are used regardless of the input size, requiring no auxiliary data structures. This results in O(1) constant space complexity.
data.takeaway: When searching for cycles or intersection points in a sequential structure without indices, use two pointers moving at different speeds to eliminate the need for a hash set.
mistakes: Failing to check if fast and fast.next are non-null before advancing, which causes a null pointer exception.
Returning true when fast or fast.next hits None instead of correctly returning false for a acyclic list.
Advancing both pointers at the same speed by accident, which prevents the fast pointer from ever catching the slow pointer in a cycle.
